Pool Tile Cleaning in Tucson, AZ: Getting the White Line Off

That chalky white band at the waterline is mineral left behind by evaporating water. One free call, any hour, puts you through to an independent, locally owned Tucson-area pool company that can look at your tile and quote the job.

Pool tile cleaning in Tucson, AZ mostly means one job: taking off the crusty white band that forms where the water meets the tile. Almost every pool in the area gets it sooner or later. This page explains what that band is made of, why Tucson's water and climate keep rebuilding it, how the common removal methods compare, what can scratch your tile, and what goes into a quote.

Tucson Pool Cleaning Pro does not clean tile. The number, (520) 372-1083, rings an automated assistant day or night. Describe your waterline, and the assistant hands the call to a local, independently owned pool business near you. The people there inspect the tile, explain how they would remove the scale, name their price and send you their bill.

What the white line on pool tile actually is

Pool water carries dissolved minerals, mainly calcium and magnesium. When the sun pulls water off the surface, only the water leaves. The minerals stay. Along the waterline the tile is wet one moment and drying the next, so a thin film keeps evaporating there and leaving a little more mineral behind each time. A pool trade article on waterline scale calls this deposit an evaporite: it builds no matter how carefully the pH is kept, because the water simply dries and the minerals cannot go with it.

Two kinds of scale show up on tile. Calcium carbonate is the common white, chalky crust. Calcium silicate forms more slowly, looks grayer and, according to pool maintenance writers, is much harder to get off. Many old scale lines are a layered mix of both, which is why a ring that has been ignored for years often needs a different method than a fresh one.

Why Tucson tile scales so quickly

Two local facts work together. First, the water going into the pool is hard. Tucson Water delivers Colorado River water brought in by the Central Arizona Project (CAP), recharged underground in Avra Valley and blended with local groundwater. The utility says the groundwater is naturally hard and that hardness rises as the share of CAP water rises. It also says hard water is safe to drink. Tucson Water does not publish one average hardness figure for the city, but its online water quality map shows readings near your address. North of the city, Oro Valley Water Utility reports hardness from 36 to 270 parts per million across its system.

Second, a lot of that water leaves by evaporation. By the Arizona Department of Water Resources' estimate, an open water surface in Tucson loses roughly six feet a year, mostly during the summer months. Every inch you top off brings in a fresh load of minerals, and every inch that evaporates leaves them in the pool. Over a few summers the pool concentrates calcium, and the tile line is where you see it first.

  • Hard fill waterCalcium arrives with every top off from the hose or autofill.
  • High evaporationAbout six feet a year leaves the minerals behind (ADWR).
  • Wet and dry cyclingSplash and small level changes keep the tile band drying over and over.
  • Unbalanced waterWater that leans toward scaling drops calcium faster on every surface.

Pool tile cleaning methods in Tucson, compared

A careful pool technician starts by looking at the scale and the tile together. How thick is the crust? Is it white and flaky or gray and glassy? Is the tile glossy glazed ceramic, glass mosaic or an older, rougher tile, and is the grout sound? The answers point to a method. The table below sums up what pool trade sources describe; the right choice for your pool is the one the company can explain to you.

Pool tile scale removal methods compared by best use, cautions and who does it
MethodBest forWatch out forWho does it
Regular brushing with a tile brushKeeping a light, fresh film from setting upWill not touch hardened scale; use a brush made for pool tile, never wireHomeowner or weekly service
Pumice or a scale scraper by handSmall patches of light carbonate scale on tough tileAbrasive; can dull glossy glaze or glass tile, slow on long tile linesAsk a pool company first
Chemical descalerCarbonate scale that is too firm to brushAcid products can etch grout and finishes and must never be mixed with other chemicals; little effect on silicateA pool professional
Media blastingHeavy or silicate scale on long tile linesMedia type and pressure decide whether glaze and grout survive; spent media must be kept out of the filterA pool company with blasting equipment

Gentle hand methods

Brushing the tile band during routine service costs little and slows a new line, and it is part of what a good weekly visit should include (see pool cleaning and weekly maintenance). Brushing will not remove scale that has hardened into a crust. Pumice is a soft volcanic stone sold for pool scale, and it works on light deposits, but it is still an abrasive. On glass tile or high gloss glaze, a scratch is permanent, so ask before you rub.

Chemical descalers

Descaling products dissolve carbonate scale. Most of them are acids, which is the reason this page gives no mixing or application steps. Acid can etch grout and cement finishes, it reacts dangerously with other pool chemicals, and the CDC warns never to mix pool chemicals with each other. A professional who uses a descaler should be able to tell you what it is, how the tile and the water will be protected, and how the pool's chemistry will be corrected afterward.

Media blasting

For thick or silicate scale, most companies use a blaster: a low pressure stream of fine media aimed at the scale band, usually with the water lowered below the tile. Trade sources describe bead blasting as a gentler cousin of sandblasting and say the right media depends on what the tile is made of. Softer media that break down on impact are aimed at taking scale off while leaving glaze alone, while harder media cut faster and can scuff glaze or erode grout. Sources in the industry do not agree on every media type, so the useful question is not "do you blast?" but "which media, at what pressure, and is it safe on my tile?" One pool industry patent filing also notes that fine blasting media can plug a pool's filtering system, so ask how spent media is cleaned up.

Not sure whether your line is light film or years of hard scale? Call and describe it. The local pool company you are put through to can look at the tile and explain which method it would use before it quotes.

What to expect on tile cleaning day

Plans vary by company, but a typical job looks something like this. The technician checks the tile and grout, agrees on the method with you and protects nearby surfaces. If the job needs it, the water is lowered below the tile band. The scale is removed section by section, the tile is rinsed and inspected, and the pool is refilled. Ask how long the work will take for your pool and whether you can swim the same evening.

If the water has to come down, it has to go somewhere. In Tucson and unincorporated Pima County the preferred route is the home's own sewer cleanout, and water may only go on the ground if it soaks in on your lot. Our guide to draining a pool in Tucson covers those rules.

A few loose tiles or cracked grout?

Cleaning sometimes shows problems the scale was hiding: hollow or loose tiles, missing grout or a crack behind the tile band. Those are repairs, not cleaning, and they can let water into the bond beam behind the tile. Ask the company to point out anything it finds, and see swimming pool repair in Tucson for what repair work involves.

Licensing. The ROC does not say plainly whether cleaning tile alone needs a contractor license, while fixing loose tile or grout is pool repair. The Arizona Registrar of Contractors (ROC) issues the R-6 license, Swimming Pool Service and Repair, for servicing and minor repairs on home pools; building pools and full interior replacement fall under licenses such as B-5. Ask any company for its ROC number, then enter it in the ROC's online contractor search to see whether the license is current, what class it is and whether complaints are on file. Apart from workers' compensation, the ROC does not require its licensees to carry insurance, so ask to see proof of liability coverage yourself.

Keeping the line from coming back

Clean tile starts collecting minerals again the day the pool is refilled. You cannot stop evaporation, but you can slow the buildup.

Helps

  • Keep the water balanced. Pool chemists use the Langelier Saturation Index (LSI), a number that shows whether water tends to dissolve or deposit calcium. The Pool and Hot Tub Alliance (PHTA) cites a range of minus 0.3 to plus 0.5 for proper balance.
  • Test the water with a home test kit and let your pool service adjust it.
  • Brush the tile band during routine cleaning.
  • Cover the pool between swims. According to ADWR, covering a pool stops 90 to 95 percent of its evaporation loss, so far less hard water gets added back.
  • Ask about a tile sealer or barrier product. Trade writers describe silicone based coatings that make it harder for calcium to bond to glaze.

Hurts

  • Letting the line go for years until it turns gray and hard.
  • Scraping with metal tools or wire brushes, which scratch the glaze.
  • Mixing pool chemicals or household cleaners. The CDC says never mix them.
  • Running the water with high pH and alkalinity for weeks.
  • Topping off again and again for years without ever diluting the water.

What moves a pool tile cleaning quote

People search for "pool tile cleaning Tucson cost" more than almost anything else about tile, so here is a straight answer: the national cost guides we checked (the large home services publishers) do not list a price for pool tile cleaning or waterline calcium removal. Any number you see online is a single company's rate, not a published range, and this page does not repeat one. Real quotes vary. These are the things that change yours:

  • Length of the tile lineA small play pool and a long lap pool with a spa spillway can have very different footage.
  • Scale thickness and typeA thin white film is quicker than a thick, gray, silicate heavy crust.
  • Method and mediaHand work, a descaler and media blasting use different time and equipment.
  • Lowering the waterWhether the level has to come down, and how far, adds time and refill water.
  • Tile and grout conditionFragile glass tile or loose grout means slower, more careful work, and repairs are priced separately.
  • Water balance afterwardSome quotes include rebalancing the refilled water; others do not.

For prices on routine pool care, see the guide to pool service cost in Tucson, which lists published ranges with their sources.

Questions to ask before tile work starts

  • Is this calcium carbonate, calcium silicate or both, and how can you tell?
  • Which method and, if blasting, which media and pressure will you use on my tile?
  • Can you try a small test area first?
  • Does the water need to be lowered, how far, and where will it be discharged?
  • How will you keep blasting media or descaler out of my filter and equipment?
  • Is rebalancing the water included in the price?
  • What is your Arizona ROC license number?

Common questions

What is the white stuff on my pool tile?

In most cases it is scale: calcium minerals that stay behind on the tile when pool water evaporates. The softer, white kind is mostly calcium carbonate. A slower forming, grayish deposit called calcium silicate can build up too, and pool trade writers describe it as much harder to remove. A pool technician can tell you which kind you have before choosing a method.

How often does Tucson pool tile need cleaning?

No published schedule fits every pool. How fast the line comes back depends on your water's hardness, how much water the pool loses to evaporation and gets topped off with, and how well the water is balanced. A practical rule: deal with the line while it is thin and still white. Thick, gray, rock hard scale takes more work to remove and raises the risk to the tile.

How much does pool tile cleaning cost in Tucson?

The national cost guides we checked do not publish a pool tile cleaning or calcium removal price, so this page does not give one. Your quote will mostly depend on how many feet of tile the pool has, how thick and hard the scale is, which removal method fits your tile and whether the water has to be lowered. Ask for the price in writing before work starts.

When cleaning pool tile, you should avoid what?

Avoid anything harder than the tile glaze: metal scrapers, wire brushes and harsh abrasives can scratch it, and scratched tile grabs scale faster. Never mix pool chemicals or cleaning products, and leave acid descalers to a professional. Ask a pool company before trying a pumice stone, because it is abrasive and not every tile can take it.

Does the pool have to be drained to clean the tile?

Not fully. Many tile jobs need the water lowered below the tile band so the scale can be reached, then the pool is topped back up. Ask the company whether your job needs that and where the water will go, because Tucson and Pima County rules decide where pool water may be discharged.

Can tile cleaning damage my pool tile?

It can if the method is too aggressive for the tile. Glass tile, glossy glazed ceramic and older grout each respond differently to abrasion and acid. Ask the company which method and which blasting media it plans to use, whether it is suited to your tile, and whether it can try a small test spot first.
